comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
## Field evidence: a store write-lock holder exceeded 60s under normal parallel agent work

Observed 2026-08-05 ~01:45 UTC during a session running several agents in parallel against
this store (each claiming, commenting, and closing tickets).

A close of d772-6007-5d04-4101 failed with:

    rebar._commands._seam.CommandError: flock: could not acquire lock after 60s
    (raised from llm/completion_sidecar.py:60 emit -> _commands/_seam.py:419 append_event)

This is direct evidence for this ticket's premise: some holder retained the store write lock
for longer than the full 60s acquisition window, starving a concurrent writer outright rather
than merely slowing it. The starved operation was a completion-sidecar append, i.e. gate
machinery, not bulk work.

Corroborating signal from the same session: an earlier `rebar review-plan` on
43ea-3d5a-078f-4fe3 computed a PASS verdict but ABORTED signing with reason
'store-read-failure' (plan_review_sign_aborted, attempt 1), and the attestation had to be
recovered separately with `rebar sign-review`. Same root condition -- contention against the
store -- surfacing in a second subsystem.

Neither failure needed an unusual workload to reproduce: it was ordinary parallel agent
activity, which is the workflow AGENTS.md actively recommends.

comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
Corroborating evidence from a high-concurrency session (2026-08-06/07), which EXTENDS this ticket's scope beyond compact-on-close.

Setup: 6-9 concurrent agents plus the live Jira reconcile bridge, all writing to this one store.

Observed failures, none of them a close/compact:
1. `rebar comment <id> ...` FAILED outright with `rebar._commands._seam.CommandError: flock: could not acquire lock after 60s`. The comment was silently lost — the command exited and the caller had to re-verify state and retry manually. So the 60s acquire timeout is reachable by ordinary writes, not just by the compact path this ticket names.
2. Immediately after, `WARNING rebar._store.push: tickets branch push-retry merge skipped: write lock busy; push stays pending`. The push deferred silently; nothing re-announced it (which is the same non-announcement mechanism proven in 2a76 — PUSH_PENDING is only computed on an explicit `rebar fsck`).
3. `rebar transition` and `rebar edit` routinely took 10-60s+ under this load, and several needed 240-550s timeouts to complete reliably.

Why this matters for the fix's shape: the ticket currently frames the problem as compact-on-close holding the lock too long. That is the biggest HOLDER, but the failure surface is wider — any writer can exhaust the 60s acquire budget and, when it does, at least one path (`comment`) surfaces it as a hard CommandError while another (push) degrades to a silent WARNING. Two consequences worth folding into the acceptance criteria:
* a writer that cannot acquire within the budget should not lose the write silently — compare ab54, which records the same class for the COMPLETION_VERDICT sidecar;
* the acquire budget is currently a fixed 60s that does not scale with contention, so adding agents makes lost writes MORE likely rather than merely slower.

Sequential single-agent operation is unaffected; this is specifically the parallel-agent workflow AGENTS.md actively encourages.

comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
OPERATOR REFRAME (2026-08-07) — this ticket's framing is wrong, and the correction changes what gets fixed.

The shared store is NOT the defect. Worktrees resolving to one lock inode via `lock.canonical_tracker` (`_store/lock.py:124-127`) is CORRECT behaviour — it is what makes concurrent writes safe, and 'isolate the stores' would trade correctness for throughput. Do not pursue that direction.

The defect is LOCK HOLD DURATION. A lock held across an entire reduce + retire + git commit (measured 2m17s on this store) would starve writers even with a single worktree. The shared inode only makes the starvation visible sooner; it is the amplifier, not the cause.

So the question this ticket must answer is: **WHY are locks held for so long, and what is the shortest correct critical section?** Not 'how do we contend less'.

Scope for the diagnosis:
* Enumerate every holder of the store write lock and measure how long each holds it, with real numbers rather than inspection. `compact-on-close` (`_commands/compact.py:178`, invoked from `transition_close.py:92-104`) is the known-biggest, but this session showed ordinary `comment`/`edit`/`transition` writes also exhausting the 60s acquire budget, so it is not the only one.
* For each holder, establish what work is INSIDE the critical section that does not need to be — git subprocess calls, network I/O, reduce/replay passes, and file writes are the usual suspects. A lock should cover the smallest mutation that must be atomic, not the whole operation that happens to contain it.
* Establish whether the 60s acquire budget is the right shape at all: it is a fixed timeout that does not scale with contention, so adding writers makes LOST WRITES more likely rather than merely slower.

REMEDIATION REQUIRES OPERATOR APPROVAL. Do not implement a fix under this ticket without it. Produce the measured diagnosis and a proposed remediation with its tradeoffs, and bring it back for a decision — narrowing a critical section is exactly the kind of change that can trade a throughput win for a correctness loss, and that call is the operator's.

Prior evidence already recorded on this ticket stands: the 2m17s compact stall, the flock 60s failure on `rebar comment`, the silent push-retry deferral, and the ab54 orphaned-sidecar fingerprint.

comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
MEASURED DIAGNOSIS (2026-08-07) — answering the operator reframe: why are locks held for so long, and what is the shortest correct critical section.

Method: a read-only clone of this store (`git clone --shared` of `.tickets-tracker` @ ef3f797170 — 3,514 ticket dirs, 47,558 event files, **71,041 commits on the `tickets` branch**) into a scratch repo with no remote, driven by an out-of-tree launcher that wraps `rebar._store.lock.acquire` / `LockHandle.release` to record acquire-wait and hold duration, plus cProfile. Nothing in the repo was modified and nothing was run against `.tickets-tracker` except read-only clone/inspection. LLM close gates were disabled in the scratch config so the numbers isolate locking, not model latency.

## 1. Measured write-lock hold times (one real store, real operations)

| Operation | Acquire site | Budget | MEASURED hold |
|---|---|---|---|
| `comment` | `event_append.py:415` `stage_and_commit` | 60s | **0.11 – 0.17s** |
| `edit` | `event_append.py:415` | 60s | **0.11s** |
| `create` | `event_append.py:415` | 60s | **0.35s** |
| `transition` (STATUS write) | `txn.py:87` ← `transition_core` (`txn.py:202`) | **30s** | **0.91s** |
| `claim` (STATUS+EDIT) | `txn.py:87` ← `claim_core` (`txn.py:336`) | **30s** | **1.79s** + a second acquire of 0.15s |
| `compact`, 1 foldable event | `compact.py:178` | 60s | **0.93s** |
| `compact`, 5 foldable / 3 signed | `compact.py:178` | 60s | **21.6s** |
| **`compact-on-close`, 7 foldable / 7 signed** | `compact.py:178` ← `transition_close.py:103` | 60s | **48.1s** |
| **`compact`, 75 foldable** | `compact.py:178` | 60s | **>20 minutes, still holding** (see §4) |

Two structural facts fall out immediately:

* **Ordinary writes are NOT long holders.** A `comment` holds the lock for ~0.13s. When `rebar comment` dies at 60s it is not because comments are slow — it is because it queued behind a compaction. The reframe is correct: hold duration is the defect, and it is concentrated in one place.
* **A close takes the lock THREE times** — `txn.transition_core` (0.91s), then `_compact_on_close` (48.1s), then `push.push_tickets_branch`'s merge leg — with the lock fully released between each. So a close is not one long section; it is one *pathological* section bracketed by two cheap ones.

## 2. What is inside `_compact_locked`, and what does not need to be

cProfile of the measured 48.1s `compact-on-close` (7 signed events):

```
_compact_locked (compact.py:166)                     48.144s   <- the whole critical section
  _build_authorship_ledger (compact.py:74)           47.767s   99.2%
    authorship.resolve_event_commit (authorship.py:131)
                                        47.475s / 7 calls = 6.78s EACH
  everything else (listdir + json parse of every event,
  reduce_ticket, SNAPSHOT atomic_write, the .retired
  renames, .cache.json unlink, git add + diff + commit)  ~0.4s
```

**The actual mutation — the thing the lock exists to make atomic — is ~0.4s. The other 47.7s is a read-only forensic query.**

`resolve_event_commit` (`attest/authorship.py:131-177`) shells out to

```
git log --diff-filter=A --full-history --no-renames --format=%H -- <ticket>/<position>-*.json
```

once **per signed folded event**, serially, holding the lock. `--full-history` disables history simplification, so each call walks the entire `tickets` branch. Measured directly against this store's history:

| history walked | wall time for one `resolve_event_commit` query |
|---|---|
| 5,000 commits | 1.23s |
| 20,000 commits | 5.92s |
| 71,041 commits (HEAD, today) | **6.23s** (ticket-scoped) |
| 71,041 commits, the **global fallback** `resolve_position_commit` (`authorship.py:180`) | **10.47s** |

So the cost of a compaction is `S × ~6.2s` (or `S × ~16.7s` when the ticket-scoped query misses and the documented global fallback fires — `compact.py:117` says the miss "can" happen at fold time). Every event this store ever writes adds a commit to the `tickets` branch, so **this term grows without bound and can only get worse**. It was ~1.2s/event when the branch had 5k commits; it is 6.2s/event at 71k.

Nothing about that query needs the lock. It reads *committed git history* about events that are *already committed*; no writer under this lock can change the answer for an event that already exists. It is inside the critical section only because it happens to sit in the middle of the function that also does the mutation.

Three smaller passengers in the same section, in descending order of concern:

* **Network I/O, reachable from inside the lock.** `identify_signer` → `_keyring_for` (`authorship.py:115`) → `rebar.show_ticket()` → `_reads._fresh` → `ticket_reads.ensure_fresh` (`_engine_support/reads.py:194`) → **`git fetch` + `sync.reconverge`**. Throttled to 1/60s by the `/tmp/.ticket-sync-*` marker, and `reconverge` then tries to take the same write lock we are holding, so it burns its full `_RECONVERGE_LOCK_TIMEOUT = 2s` self-blocked and gives up. Bounded (fetch RTT + 2s per 60s window) but it is genuinely a network call and a self-contended lock acquire inside the critical section. Not measured here — the scratch clone has no remote, so this path no-op'd; the code path is unconditional on a store that does have one.
* `_keyring_for` is **not memoized** — it re-reduces the identity ticket once per signed event.
* `_build_authorship_ledger` also re-reads and re-parses every event file that the pass at `compact.py:193-210` already read and parsed.

## 3. What is inside the OTHER critical sections that does not need to be

`txn.py` (claim/transition, 30s budget) is the only other site with avoidable work of any size:

* `finalize_event` → `_seam.attribution_fields` → `identity.resolve_current_identity` → `_match_by_email` (`_commands/identity.py:119`) **reduces ALL 3,515 tickets in the store** — measured 0.68s, inside the lock. It is O(store size), so it grows with the store the way the git walk grows with history. Note the asymmetry: on the `event_append` path `finalize_event` runs *before* the lock (which is why `comment` is 0.13s); on the `txn` path it runs *inside* it.
* `hlc.next_tick` is a **nested lock acquisition** (`.rebar/hlc.lock` RMW) inside the store lock at `txn.py:272`, `txn.py:365` and `txn.py:397` (twice in one claim). `inbound_translate.py:246` deliberately hoists the identical call *outside* — the same call, two opposite decisions.
* On a gated close the ticket is **reduced twice** under one lock: `txn.py:205`, then again inside `pre_status_check` → `signing.verify_signature` → `_resolve_and_reduce`.

Everything genuinely expensive elsewhere is already outside the lock and should stay there — `git push` and `git fetch` are both explicitly hoisted (`push.py:250-252`, `sync.py:227`), and no LLM call is inside any critical section. `push`'s merge leg (15s budget) and `sync.reconverge` (15s) hold only local `git merge` / `stash` / `reset --hard`; `fsck_repair.py:236` holds a 60s budget for a pure rename loop; `inbound_translate.py:283` holds two syscalls.

## 4. The contention reproduction — this is how writes are LOST, measured

One holder (`rebar compact` on a 75-event ticket, the `compact-on-close` class) plus 6 concurrent `rebar comment` writers against the same store, started 3s after the holder:

```
writer 1 FAIL elapsed=62.13s     flock: could not acquire lock after 60s
writer 2 FAIL elapsed=62.12s
writer 3 FAIL elapsed=62.12s
writer 4 FAIL elapsed=62.12s
writer 5 FAIL elapsed=62.09s
writer 6 FAIL elapsed=62.16s
```

**6 of 6 concurrent writes were lost.** Not delayed — lost: `LockTimeout` is terminal, there is no retry, no queue and no durable spool, and `rebar show` on the target ticket afterwards shows none of the six comments. This is a byte-for-byte reproduction of the field report already on this ticket (`rebar comment` → `flock: could not acquire lock after 60s`), and of the ab54 fingerprint (the same failure on the best-effort `COMPLETION_VERDICT` sidecar, where it is swallowed at `completion_sidecar.py:61-65` and returns `False`, so the write is lost *silently*).

An unrelated `rebar claim` issued during the same window died at **30s**, not 60 — `txn.py:87` passes `attempts=1`. So the budgets are asymmetric: a holder allowed 60s can starve a claimer allowed only 30s.

The holder was still holding after **20 minutes** at the time of writing. 75 events × ~6.7s/event ≈ 8.4 minutes of pure `git log` walking, plus the fallback query where the ticket-scoped one missed.

## 5. Answering the ticket's question directly

**Why are locks held for so long?** One reason, dominating everything else by two orders of magnitude: `_build_authorship_ledger` runs a per-event, full-history `git log` walk inside the compaction critical section, and that walk's cost grows linearly with the tracker's commit count. Secondarily: identity resolution reduces the whole store inside the `txn` lock, and a `git fetch` is reachable from inside the compaction lock.

**What is the shortest correct critical section?** For compaction: the SNAPSHOT write + the `.retired` renames + the `git add`/`commit` — **~0.4s measured**, against 48.1s today. Everything else in `_compact_locked` is either a read of already-committed state (the ledger's git walks, the signer verification) or a re-parse of data already read. For `txn`: reduce → guard → HLC tick → atomic_write → add → commit, with identity/attribution resolved before the lock as the `event_append` path already does.

**Corroborating side-effect observed:** a concurrent reader's reducer cache write failed mid-compaction (`reducer/_cache.py:146`, `FileNotFoundError` renaming `.cache.json.tmp`) because compaction deletes `.cache.json` at `compact.py:365-368` while readers — which take no lock — are writing it. Benign (the cache is regenerable) but it is a second, independent race the long hold widens.

Instrumentation note: the wrapper used for these numbers lives entirely outside the repo and changes no rebar behaviour. If the operator wants these numbers on tap in production, the landable-independently observability slice is (a) a `REBAR_LOCK_TRACE` env that logs acquire-wait + hold-duration + call site at DEBUG from `lock.acquire`/`LockHandle.release`, and (b) making `LockTimeout` read `.ticket-write.lock.d/owner` before giving up so a starved waiter can name its blocker (this ticket's AC2). Both are pure observability and carry no locking-behaviour change.

comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
ASSESSMENT OF THE 60s ACQUIRE BUDGET, AND A RANKED REMEDIATION PROPOSAL — FOR OPERATOR APPROVAL. Nothing here is implemented; no change altering locking behaviour has been pushed.

## A. Is a fixed timeout the right shape?

**The budgets are inconsistent and inverted relative to the work they guard.**

| site | budget | measured/structural work held |
|---|---|---|
| `event_append.stage_and_commit` / `batch` / `delete_events` | 60s (30×2) | 0.11–0.35s |
| `txn._acquire_write_lock` (claim, transition) | **30s** (30×1) | 0.9–1.8s |
| `compact._compact_locked` | 60s | **21.6s – >13min** |
| `ensures.run_ensures` | 60s | up to 3 `git commit`s |
| `purge_bridge._commit_deletion` | 60s | one bulk `git add`+`commit` |
| `fsck_repair._repair_ticket` | 60s | a rename loop (milliseconds) |
| `push` merge leg | 15s | local `git merge` (+`stash`/`pop`) |
| `sync.reconverge` | 15s | local `git merge` / `reset --hard` |
| `inbound_translate` | 30s | two syscalls |

The cheapest sections carry the largest budgets; the only genuinely long holder carries the same 60s as a 0.13s comment; and `claim` — the operation AGENTS.md tells every agent to run FIRST — carries the *smallest* budget of any foreground write. A holder permitted 60s can therefore starve a claimer permitted 30s deterministically, which is exactly what happened during measurement.

**The waiters are a lottery, not a queue.** `_acquire_fcntl` polls `LOCK_EX|LOCK_NB` with a jittered 50ms sleep (`lock.py:170-186`); `_acquire_mkdir` polls `mkdir` with a jittered 100ms sleep (`lock.py:412-441`). There is no FIFO ordering and no ticketing. With W waiters each release round is won by roughly one of them at random, so expected wait grows with W while the deadline stays fixed. P(timeout) therefore **rises with concurrency**.

**Exceeding the budget is terminal and lossy, not slow.** `LockTimeout` has no retry, no backoff-and-requeue, and no durable spool: `stage_and_commit` unlinks the staging temp and raises. The CLI turns that into `CommandError` (write lost, operator must notice and retry); best-effort emitters — the `COMPLETION_VERDICT` sidecar (`completion_sidecar.py:61-65`), the push-retry merge (`push.py:355`) — swallow it and the write is lost *silently*. Measured: 6 concurrent `comment`s under one holder, 6 lost.

So: for an append-only event store whose entire value proposition is that every write is a durable shared record, **a fixed deadline whose expiry destroys the write is the wrong failure shape**. Latency under contention is acceptable; data loss under contention is not. That is the real defect in the budget, more than the number 60.

**The alternatives, with tradeoffs:**

1. **Keep the fixed timeout, change what expiry means** — on `LockTimeout`, leave the canonical event in a durable pending spool and let the next successful writer (or `rebar fsck`) adopt and commit it. Events are UUID-keyed and merge by union, so a late commit is safe by construction. *Cost:* a new durable state ("written but not yet committed"), and a genuine semantic change — a caller that saw a failure could later find its write present ("phantom write"). Needs the operator's judgement, not just a patch.
2. **Fair queueing (FIFO ticket lock)** — numbered waiters, each takes its turn. Makes wait time `queue position × hold time` instead of a lottery, so a deadline becomes a *meaningful* statement about queue depth. *Cost:* real complexity in the most safety-critical file in the repo, plus stale-ticket reaping, and it must preserve the dual-window fcntl+mkdir contract that `lock.py`'s module docstring calls permanent.
3. **Adaptive budget** — scale the deadline with observed contention, or wait indefinitely as long as the *holder identity changes* (i.e. the system is making progress) and only fail on a genuinely wedged holder. *Cost:* it hides the real defect behind patience, and unbounded waits are their own operational hazard.
4. **Blocking `flock(LOCK_EX)` under a SIGALRM deadline** instead of NB-polling — the kernel queues waiters, which is fairer than polling. *Cost:* flock wakeup order is unspecified on macOS anyway, and the mkdir leg still polls, so it buys less than it looks.
5. **Change nothing about the budget; just shrink the holder.** *Cost:* does not change the failure shape at all — at high enough concurrency writes are still lost. But it is the cheapest change by far and, on the measured numbers, it removes every incident this ticket records.

**My reading:** option 5 first, because a 100× reduction in the only long holder is available for a small, well-fenced change, and because until it lands any budget work is tuning around a bug. Then re-measure with the same 6-writer harness. If writes still fail, the right next step is option 1 (make loss impossible), not option 2/3 (make waiting longer) — the goal is "no write is ever lost", not "waits are fairer".

## B. Ranked remediation proposal

Ranked by measured benefit ÷ risk. Each names where it could break atomicity and the test that would prove it does not.

### R1 — Batch the introducing-commit resolution into ONE history walk (highest benefit, lowest risk)
`_build_authorship_ledger` calls `resolve_event_commit` once per signed event, each a full `--full-history` walk. A single walk scoped to the ticket dir with `--name-only` yields the introducing commit for *every* event in one pass.
* **Measured benefit:** 7 walks × 6.78s → 1 walk ≈ 6.8s. On the 75-event case, ~500s → ~7s. Also removes the `S × 10.5s` global-fallback tail.
* **Atomicity risk:** none — this is a pure refactor of a read-only query; the lock is untouched and the section still covers everything it covers today.
* **Proof:** a differential test asserting the batched resolver returns byte-identical `commit_sha` to `resolve_event_commit`/`resolve_position_commit` for every event of a fixture store with a non-trivial (merged, compacted) history, including the case the current ticket-scoped query misses and the global fallback catches. The existing `verify-authorship` suite must stay green on a store compacted through the new path.

### R2 — Hoist the ledger OUT of the critical section
Compute the ledger before `lock.acquire`, then inside the lock verify the fold set is unchanged; on mismatch, recompute the delta for the new events or defer the pass.
* **Measured benefit:** with R1 this takes the section from 48.1s to ~0.4s (the mutation only). Without R1 it still takes it to ~0.4s but moves 47s of work to an unlocked phase that may have to be redone.
* **Atomicity risk — the part needing care:** the ledger must describe exactly the set of events actually folded. If an append lands between the pre-lock scan and the in-lock decision, a stale ledger either omits a folded signed event (`verify-authorship` then cannot re-verify it — a real correctness loss) or includes one that stayed live (harmless duplicate). The guard is a cheap in-lock equality check on the sorted `(uuid, size, mtime)` set of fold candidates.
* **Proof:** (i) a failpoint test in the shape of the existing `REBAR_TEST_COMPACT_RENAME_BARRIER` that injects an append between scan and lock and asserts the pass either aborts cleanly or produces a ledger whose entries are exactly the folded signed events; (ii) an invariant test over random fold sets: `{ledger entries} == {folded events with author_sig}`; (iii) a two-process test that appends continuously while compacting in a loop, asserting no event is ever folded without a matching ledger entry.

### R3 — Make compact-on-close lock-POLITE (smallest change here; independent of R1/R2)
`_compact_on_close` currently acquires with the full 60s budget. Compaction is pure maintenance — skipping a pass costs nothing durable, because it re-fires on the next close and on `compact-all`. Acquire with a short budget (e.g. `timeout=5, attempts=1`) and skip silently when busy.
* **Benefit:** a close can no longer queue for a minute behind another close's compaction; the failure mode becomes "compaction deferred" instead of "close blocked". It also bounds the damage if R1/R2 are deferred.
* **Atomicity risk:** none to the store. The risk is *policy*: event logs stay uncompacted longer under sustained load, so `compact-all` needs to actually run. Worth pairing with a metric.
* **Proof:** a test that holds the lock, closes a ticket, and asserts the close succeeds, the ticket is uncompacted, and a later `compact` folds it identically.

### R4 — Hoist identity/attribution resolution out of the `txn` critical section
`_match_by_email` reduces all 3,515 tickets inside the `txn` lock (0.68s measured, O(store)). The `event_append` path already resolves it before the lock.
* **Benefit:** small today (~0.7s of a 30s budget) but it is the same unbounded-growth shape as R1, and it removes an inconsistency between two write paths.
* **Atomicity risk:** the resolved identity must be the one in force when the event is finalized. It is derived from git config plus the identity registry, neither of which this lock protects, so the exposure is a registry edit racing the write — already possible today on the `event_append` path.
* **Proof:** assert the finalized event's `author_email`/`author_id` are identical resolved inside vs outside the lock across the fixture matrix; plus a test that mutates the identity registry mid-write and asserts the documented deterministic choice.

### R5 — Give `LockTimeout` a holder identity (this ticket's AC2; pure observability)
On timeout, read `.ticket-write.lock.d/owner` and include the v2 stamp (pid, host) and the lock dir's age in the exception message. Optionally a `REBAR_LOCK_TRACE` DEBUG log of acquire-wait + hold + call site.
* **Benefit:** the 2m17s holder on this ticket was identified by inferring from a commit timeline. That should be one line of stderr.
* **Risk:** none — no behaviour change; the stamp is best-effort and may be absent (report "unknown holder").
* **Proof:** a test that holds the lock in a child process and asserts the waiter's `LockTimeout` message names that pid.
* **Landable independently of every other item here.**

### R6 — Change what a lost write means (needs an explicit operator decision, not just approval)
Option A.1 above: spool-and-adopt instead of unlink-and-raise, so a `LockTimeout` costs latency rather than data. This is what would actually close ab54 and the silent-loss half of e1ed's class, and it is the only item that survives arbitrary concurrency.
* **Risk:** introduces "phantom write" semantics (a caller that saw a failure may later find the write landed). That is a user-visible contract change and is the operator's call, not mine.
* **Proof:** kill a writer mid-timeout and assert the event either lands exactly once or is reported as pending by `rebar fsck`; a fuzz test with N writers and a forced-contention holder asserting `writes_attempted == writes_landed + writes_reported_pending`, with zero silently dropped.

### Not recommended
* Store isolation per worktree — ruled out by the operator reframe, and the measurements support that: with a single worktree, a 48s–13min hold starves anything.
* Raising the 60s budget — it would have converted the measured 6/6 losses into 6/6 minute-long stalls, and the >13-minute holder would have blown through any plausible number anyway.
* Splitting the compaction commit or the claim's STATUS+EDIT commit — both are load-bearing atomicity (`txn.py:324-331` documents that no reader may see `in_progress` without an assignee), and neither is where the time goes.

## C. Suggested sequencing

R5 (observability, land alone) → R1 (pure query refactor, big measured win, no lock semantics touched) → R3 (three lines, bounds the blast radius) → re-run the 6-writer contention harness → R2 (the real fix for the critical section, and the one that needs the failpoint tests) → R4 → then, and only with fresh measurements in hand, decide on R6 and on whether the budget shape itself needs changing.

Awaiting the operator's decision. Ticket left OPEN.

comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
ADDENDUM — R1's benefit is now MEASURED, and it is larger than I estimated.

R1 proposed replacing `_build_authorship_ledger`'s per-event `resolve_event_commit` walks with a single batched history walk. Measured on the same clone (71,041 commits on the tickets branch), resolving the introducing commit for EVERY event of a ticket in one pass with a DIRECTORY-scoped pathspec:

    git -c log.showSignature=false log --diff-filter=A --full-history --no-renames \
        --format='C %H' --name-only -- <ticket-id>/

| ticket | files resolved | batched walk | current per-event cost |
|---|---|---|---|
| 030f-c14f-596a-4f79 | 18 | **0.53s** | 7 signed x 6.78s = 47.5s (the profiled close) |
| c97f-90ae-4976-47c7 | 159 | **3.83s** | ~115 x 6.2s ≈ 712s |

That is **90x** on the profiled close and **~186x** on the larger ticket, and the batched form's cost is per-COMPACTION rather than per-EVENT, so it stops scaling with the number of signed events entirely.

The reason for the gap is worth recording because it is the actual mechanism, not just a batching win: today's pathspec is a per-file GLOB (`<dir>/<position>-*.json`, `authorship.py:151`), and a wildcard forces git to evaluate the match at every commit; a bare directory prefix lets git prune whole trees. The global fallback (`authorship.py:180`, pathspec `*<position>-*.json`) is worse still for the same reason — measured 10.47s per call.

Implication for the ranking on this ticket: **R1 alone takes the profiled compact-on-close critical section from 48.1s to roughly 1.0s** — i.e. below the 15s budget `push`'s merge leg gets, and far below the 60s that the six measured writers lost their writes to. R2 (hoisting the ledger out of the lock entirely) would take it the rest of the way to the ~0.4s of actual mutation, but on these numbers R1 is the change that ends the incident class, and it is a pure refactor of a read-only query with no lock-semantics change and no atomicity exposure. That strengthens the case for the sequencing already proposed (R5 -> R1 -> R3 -> re-measure -> R2).

Still awaiting operator approval; nothing implemented.

comments.body:
CORRECTION to the measured diagnosis: the 75-event compaction's hold time is **488.2s (8m08s)**, not the '>20 minutes, still holding' I recorded while the run was in flight. My liveness check was `pgrep -f 'rebar_probe.py compact'`, whose pattern matched my own shell command line, so it reported RUNNING after the compactor had already exited. The instrumented figure is authoritative:

    {"argv": ["compact", "6118-8fb2-774f-4c5c"], "site": "compact.py:178:_compact_locked",
     "wait_s": 0.0004, "hold_s": 488.2131, "outcome": "ok"}

488.2s for 75 foldable events is 6.5s/event, which matches the per-event `resolve_event_commit` cost measured independently (6.23s ticket-scoped) and confirms the model: compaction hold time is `S x ~6.5s` plus ~0.4s of actual mutation, with S the number of signed folded events.

Nothing else in the diagnosis changes — in particular the contention result stands exactly as recorded: during that 488s hold, 6 of 6 concurrent `rebar comment` writers failed at 60s and all six writes were permanently lost. 488s against a 60s budget means an 8x overrun, so every writer arriving in the first ~7 minutes of that window loses its write. The field 2m17s gap already on this ticket is the same phenomenon at a smaller S.

comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
OPERATOR DECISION (2026-08-07): R5 and R1 APPROVED. R3 deferred pending a design answer. R2/R4/R6 not approved.

**R5 — approved.** Extend the mkdir ownership stamp, which is already versioned (`rebar-lock v2 host=<host> ns=<pid-ns> pid=<pid> start=<start-time>`) and whose reader is documented to decline gracefully on an unparseable shape — so this is a v3 field addition, not new machinery. Add, in order of usefulness: the OPERATION/verb (compact-on-close vs comment — what held it is more actionable than which ticket), the SESSION id (resolvable via `_commands/session_id.py:37-41`'s precedence tuple), and the TICKET id (available at txn/compact call sites but NOT in the lock API — `acquire(tracker, ...)` takes no ticket, so it needs a parameter). Any field that cannot be resolved must be omitted rather than guessed.

**R1 — approved.** Replace the per-event `git log --diff-filter=A --full-history` in `resolve_event_commit` (`attest/authorship.py:131`) with one directory-scoped walk. Measured 90x (0.53s vs 47.5s for one ticket's 18 files) and 186x on a 159-file ticket; the profiled 48.1s close drops to ~1.0s. The mechanism is that the per-file GLOB pathspec defeats git's tree pruning. Read-only refactor; no lock semantics touched.

**R3 — DEFERRED, pending a design answer, not rejected.** Detection needs no new mechanism: `_acquire_fcntl` already polls `fcntl.flock(LOCK_EX|LOCK_NB)`, so a single non-blocking probe answers 'is it busy'. It must cover BOTH legs (fcntl and mkdir) and release the first if the second fails. The unanswered question is what happens to SKIPPED compaction: under sustained load it could be deferred indefinitely, so it needs a floor (force after N skips, or delegate to a scheduled path). Decide that before implementing.

**R2 — NOT approved, and R1 makes it unnecessary.** The race it would introduce is real: the ledger maps each signed event to its introducing commit for `verify-authorship`; computed outside the lock, a concurrent append or compact can change the fold set in between, yielding a STALE LEDGER THAT OMITS A FOLDED SIGNED EVENT — an attestation-chain correctness failure, not a performance one. Mitigable by compare-and-swap (recheck the fold set in-lock, recompute on change), but at ~0.5s post-R1 there is no reason to move it out at all. Keeping it inside the lock preserves atomicity for free.

**Architectural questions asked and answered (for the record, NOT approved work):**

*Per-worktree copies of the tickets branch, letting git merge on push* — partially sound. Event files are `{timestamp}-{uuid}-{TYPE}.json` under per-ticket dirs, so APPENDS ARE ALREADY CONFLICT-FREE BY CONSTRUCTION (disjoint paths). Three blockers: compaction RENAMES to `.retired` and writes SNAPSHOTs, so two clones compacting one ticket give git rename-vs-rename it cannot resolve; shared mutable files (`bindings.json`, `.bridge_state/`, `.store-compat.json` — note 0241 already proposes moving `.bridge_state/` off-branch for this reason); and compaction is not commutative, so 'let git resolve it' has no correct answer when both sides folded differently. Viable only if compaction is centralised to one writer AND shared files move off-branch.

*Per-ticket lock instead of per-repo* — structurally the right direction. The logical mutation IS per-ticket. Constraint: `git add`/`git commit` are repo-global (index.lock), so the commit step must serialise regardless. HLC is NOT a blocker — it already holds its own short dedicated lock on `.rebar/hlc.lock` and its state is an explicitly disposable cache. Shape: per-ticket lock for the mutation + a brief global lock for stage+commit, or per-ticket locks feeding `batch_stage_and_commit` (`event_append.py:479`), which ALREADY EXISTS and already documents the minimal-critical-section pattern ('validated and canonical-staged BEFORE the lock is taken; then, holding the single write lock exactly ONCE, each staged temp is atomically renamed'). Sequence it AFTER R1 and re-measure: at ~1s holds, six concurrent writers fit inside a 60s budget with room to spare, which may remove the need entirely.

Note `compact` is the outlier against this codebase's own established pattern — `batch_stage_and_commit` does its expensive work outside the lock; `compact` does 47s of read-only git archaeology inside it.

comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
OPERATOR DECISIONS, round 2 (2026-08-07):

**R5 — approved WITH EXISTING MACHINERY.** Scope narrowed from my earlier proposal: do NOT bump the stamp to v3, do NOT thread a ticket parameter through `lock.acquire`, do NOT wire in session-id resolution. Surface what the stamp ALREADY carries — `rebar-lock v2 host=<host-identity> ns=<pid-ns-id> pid=<pid> start=<start-time>` — which `LockTimeout` currently reads and discards. host+pid+start is enough to identify the holder and to distinguish a live holder from a stale stamp. The absent/unreadable/declined-shape case must say so plainly rather than printing a partial line.

**R3 — APPROVED.** The blocking objection was that skipped compaction could defer indefinitely under sustained load. The operator reports the load is INTERMITTENT, not sustained, which removes it: a skipped compaction is picked up by a later uncontended run, so no forced-after-N-skips floor is needed. Detection needs no new mechanism (`_acquire_fcntl` already polls `fcntl.flock(LOCK_EX|LOCK_NB)`); the probe must cover both legs and release the first if the second fails; the skip must be a correctness no-op and must be logged findably.

**Per-ticket locking — recorded as a FUTURE CONSIDERATION**, explicitly deferred to a second round IF this remediation does not deliver the needed improvement. Not approved now. The analysis stands for whoever picks it up: the logical mutation is per-ticket and HLC is not a blocker (own short lock on `.rebar/hlc.lock`, state is a disposable cache), but `git add`/`git commit` are repo-global so the commit step serialises regardless; the shape would be a per-ticket lock for the mutation plus a brief global lock for stage+commit, or per-ticket locks feeding the existing `batch_stage_and_commit` (`event_append.py:479`). Re-measure after R1 before deciding — at ~1s holds, six concurrent writers fit inside a 60s budget with room to spare, which may retire the question entirely.

---

**ANSWER TO THE OPERATOR'S QUESTION — how compaction renames and shared mutable files are handled today under parallel clients.** Answer: renames are PREVENTED locally rather than merged, and are UNHANDLED across clones. Three distinct mechanisms, only two of which are policies:

1. **Event appends — no policy needed, by construction.** The tickets-branch `.gitattributes` states it outright: 'uuid-named ticket dirs never collide, so they never need a merge policy'. Files are `{timestamp}-{uuid}-{TYPE}.json` under per-ticket dirs, so two clients appending produce disjoint paths that merge trivially.

2. **Shared mutable root files — `merge=ours`.** `.bridge_state/* merge=ours` on the tickets branch, with the rationale committed alongside it: these are 'per-pass derived CACHES the reconciler rebuilds, not ticket events', so on a union reconverge we keep our copy and let the next pass rebuild the loser. The comment also records that `merge=union` is WRONG here because it line-unions JSON into invalid JSON. IMPORTANT FRAGILITY: the 'ours' driver must be defined in git config by init (`merge.ours.driver=true`); without it these patterns are SILENTLY IGNORED.

3. **Compaction renames — no merge handling at all.** There is no rename/retired-specific logic anywhere in the push path. Locally this never arises: every worktree resolves to ONE store through `lock.canonical_tracker`, so the write lock serialises all local writers — the race is PREVENTED, not resolved. Across CLONES (e.g. the GitHub Actions reconciler vs a local agent) a concurrent compaction of the same ticket lands in the push path's terminal branch: '# Real content conflict — retry won't help, but continue so _MAX_RETRIES is honored', which aborts the merge, warns, exhausts retries, and leaves the push PENDING. Nothing auto-resolves it.

This is precisely why the per-worktree-clone idea is unsafe as posed: it would convert case 3 from a PREVENTED race into an UNHANDLED one, at the frequency of every parallel agent rather than the rare cross-clone case. The single shared store plus one write lock is what makes compaction safe today — which is why the operator's reframe (the defect is hold DURATION, not the shared store) is the correct one.

comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
OPERATOR QUESTIONS, round 3 — design answers (analysis only; NOT approved work).

**Q: how do we make the `ours` driver's failure loud instead of silently ignored?**

First, a correction to the framing: the driver is not merely 'set by init and hopefully still there'. `init.py:5-6` records that the ensure registry NORMALIZES merge-driver configuration, and an existing tracker 'self-heals on any ensure sweep' (`init.py:132`). So a healthy store re-converges it. The real gap is that NOTHING VERIFIES THE ATTRIBUTE AND THE DRIVER AGREE — `.gitattributes` can name a driver that git config does not define, and git then silently ignores the attribute.

Three levels, strongest first:

1. **Test the EFFECT, not the configuration.** In a scratch store, construct a real merge conflict on a `.bridge_state/*` path and assert our copy won. If the driver is undefined the merge conflicts and the test fails. A config assertion is a CLAIM that a setting exists; an actual merge is PROOF the behaviour works. This session produced the same lesson twice — 599e (an entire test surface passing by not running) and 24f7 (a tree-wide grep run once by hand instead of committed as a test).
2. **Derive the check from `.gitattributes`, do not hardcode 'ours'.** Parse every `merge=<name>` pattern and assert each `<name>` is defined in git config. That catches a FUTURE `merge=foo` added without its driver, which a hardcoded ours-check would miss.
3. **Make the ensure sweep report when it had to fix it** (APPLIED vs already-ok). Self-healing that is silent hides the fact that something upstream keeps stripping the config.

**Q: how can compaction conflicts self-heal, given compaction is deterministic?**

The determinism holds for CONTENT but not for IDENTITY, and that distinction is where the fix lives. `compiled_state` is derived from the same events, and the code already drops non-deterministic keys (`updated_at`) before persisting (`compact.py:138`) — so content-determinism is already deliberately pursued. But each SNAPSHOT is an EVENT carrying its own `uuid`, so two clients folding an IDENTICAL event set emit DIFFERENT filenames. They do not conflict; they duplicate.

Four moves, in order of leverage:

1. **Content-address the SNAPSHOT.** Name it by a hash of the folded event set + `compiled_state` rather than a fresh uuid. Two clients folding the same set then write a BYTE-IDENTICAL file at the SAME path, which git merges cleanly as 'both added identical content'. Different fold sets hash differently and both land harmlessly. This is the smallest change that cashes in the determinism, and it turns the deterministic case from a conflict into a non-event.
2. **Treat compaction output as a DERIVED CACHE** — the identical policy already applied to `.bridge_state/*`. The event log is the source of truth; the snapshot is an optimization. On conflict: keep the union of live events, discard BOTH snapshots, let the next compaction rebuild. Losing a compaction costs disk, never correctness.
3. **Bias resolution toward KEEPING events.** Uncompacted state is always semantically valid, so the safe direction is resurrect, never retire. That makes the rule provably lossless — worst case is redundant work on the next pass.
4. Longer term, centralise compaction to a single writer, which removes the cross-clone race rather than resolving it.

**HAZARD that any of these must respect:** resolution has to be ATOMIC OVER THE PAIR (the SNAPSHOT and its `.retired` renames), not per-file. A per-file `merge=ours` would happily take OUR snapshot alongside THEIR retirements, dropping events our snapshot never folded. So this needs a custom merge driver or a post-merge repair that reasons about the pair — a `.gitattributes` line cannot express it.

Also worth noting for whoever implements: `compact.py:65` already contemplates 'a remote SNAPSHOT written by another agent is visible and local compaction can ...', and `compact.py:150` handles the mid-retirement crash window (SNAPSHOT written, retirement incomplete). Both are adjacent to this problem and should be read before designing the merge behaviour.

comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
PRIOR-ART RESEARCH on content-addressing the SNAPSHOT (operator-requested). Conclusion: content-addressing is a real but PARTIAL win, and the domain-matched prior art solved this a different way. This CORRECTS my earlier ranking, which put content-addressing first.

**1. The closest prior art — git-bug — did NOT use content-addressed snapshots. It removed the need to merge at all.**
git-bug is a distributed, offline-first issue tracker embedded in git: the same problem shape as rebar (tickets in git, multiple clients, offline edits, sync via push/pull). Its design uses LAMPORT TIMESTAMPS plus an OPERATION-BASED DATA MODEL so concurrent edits from multiple remotes merge WITHOUT conflicts and without manual resolution. It also stores data as git OBJECTS under a ref namespace (refs/bugs) rather than as worktree files, so git's file-merge semantics never apply in the first place.
Relevance: rebar is already most of the way there — an append-only event log plus an HLC (same family as Lamport clocks). Our own ticket e3d0 already cites the 'git-bug operationPack pattern'. The divergence is that rebar MATERIALISES events as worktree FILES, which is what drags git's merge semantics into the picture. The SNAPSHOT is the one artifact in our store that is not conflict-free by construction.

**2. The cautionary tale — Nix content-addressed derivations — is the same bet we were about to make, and it has not paid off yet.**
CA derivations (RFC 0062) remain EXPERIMENTAL and opt-in years later; the stabilisation milestone was ~65% complete as of March 2026. The blockers are precisely the ones our design would inherit:
* **Determinism does not hold in practice.** Reported in the haskell.nix tutorial: 'ghc is deterministic only disabling the parallel building i.e. passing -j1'. Real producers leak non-determinism through ordering and parallelism.
* **Divergent realisations poison the cache.** The current implementation 'just forbids fetching a path if the local system has a different realisation for the same drv output ... it can result in a totally useless binary cache in some pathological cases'. That is the exact failure our snapshot would hit if determinism leaks: two byte-different artifacts claiming to be the same logical thing, and NO RULE to choose between them — strictly worse than the conflict we set out to avoid, because both look correct.
* CI infrastructure (Hydra) still does not support it.

**3. Where content-addressing DOES succeed, the artifacts are never merged.**
Bazel's remote cache is a content-addressable store of build outputs; OCI/Docker layers and git's own object database are the same pattern. In every one, artifacts are IMMUTABLE and simply coexist — content addressing solves IDENTITY and DEDUPLICATION, not CONFLICT RESOLUTION. Nobody merges two blobs.
That is the decisive distinction for us: our problem is a MERGE problem. Content-addressing the snapshot removes only the SPURIOUS conflict (two clients folding an identical event set). The conflict we actually care about — DIVERGENT FOLD SETS — is untouched by it, because different inputs legitimately hash differently and both land.

**Revised recommendation.** Promote what was option 2 to first: treat the SNAPSHOT as a DERIVED CACHE and regenerate on conflict (union the live events, discard both snapshots, let the next compaction rebuild) — a derived cache never needs to merge, which is the same insight that makes git-bug's model work and the same policy already applied to `.bridge_state/*`. Content-addressing drops to a COMPLEMENTARY dedup win: cheap, safe, removes the spurious-collision case, but not a conflict-resolution strategy on its own. And if we do content-address, Nix's experience says the prerequisite is proving determinism holds under parallelism and ordering — `compact.py:138` already strips `updated_at`, but that is one key, not a proof.

Sources: NixOS/nix milestone 35 (ca-derivations stabilisation); NixOS RFC 0062 content-addressed paths; haskell.nix CA-derivations tutorial; NixOS wiki ca-derivations; git-bug (github.com/git-bug/git-bug); Bazel remote caching docs.

comments.author: RebarBotNava
comments.body:
LANDED (2026-08-07): the two operator-approved remediations, plus R3 after its design answer. Ticket left OPEN — the operator owns its disposition.

## What landed

| | change | what it does |
|---|---|---|
| R5 | Gerrit 1507 | a `LockTimeout` NAMES the holder |
| R1 | Gerrit 1508 | one directory-scoped git walk per compaction instead of one full-history walk per signed event |
| R3 | Gerrit 1510 | compact-on-close stands aside when the write lock is already busy |

R2, R4 and R6 remain unimplemented (not approved). Per-ticket locking was NOT started — recorded as the future consideration if this round does not deliver.

## R5 — what the timeout now says

Scoped by the operator to EXISTING machinery: no v3 stamp, no new fields, no session-id
resolution, no new parameter on `lock.acquire`. The mkdir leg already wrote
`rebar-lock v2 host=<host-identity> ns=<pid-ns> pid=<pid> start=<start-time>` and the
timeout threw it away. `describe_lock_holder()` now renders it, and `LockTimeout`
appends it:

    flock: could not acquire lock after 60s
        (holder: host=name-h pid=4321 start=93117 held=48s pid_state=live)

`pid_state` is the second question a starved writer has — is a process really holding
this, or is the stamp stale — and it follows the same refusal-without-proof rule
reclamation uses (`unprobeable (foreign host)` / `unprobeable (other pid namespace)`),
so the message can never suggest a reclaim the lock itself would refuse. Every case the
stamp cannot answer is stated plainly rather than guessed: `unknown (no ownership
stamp)`, `unknown (unrecognised ownership stamp)` (the documented forward-compat decline
path), `unknown (incomplete ownership stamp)` (a torn mid-write read). The bash-parity
message prefix is unchanged, and an unreadable stamp degrades to exactly the old string.

## R1 — measured before/after on the real-sized store

Measured against the read-only 71,041-commit clone (`/tmp/lockbig/.tickets-tracker`),
resolving the introducing commit for every event of a ticket. OLD = one
`resolve_event_commit` full-history walk per event; NEW = one
`build_ticket_position_commit_map` directory-scoped walk for the whole ticket:

| ticket | files | OLD (per-event) | NEW (one walk) | speedup | mismatches |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 030f-c14f-596a-4f79 | 4 | 29.81s | 1.05s | 28x | 0 |
| df2c-e4b8-496d-4698 | 25 | 193.16s | 4.72s | 41x | 0 |
| c97f-90ae-4976-47c7 | 73 | 546.00s | 4.27s | 128x | 0 |
| 5200-e04e-246e-4aae | 155 | **1165.54s** | **2.09s** | **557x** | 0 |

257 events resolved across the four tickets, **0 mismatches** — the batched map returned
a byte-identical commit sha to `resolve_event_commit` for every single one, on the real
71k-commit history.

The OLD column is the compaction hold time this ticket measured as the defect: 155 events
is 1165s (19m26s) of read-only git archaeology holding the store write lock, against a 60s
acquire budget. It is now 2.09s. Note the NEW column does not grow with the event count —
it is one directory-scoped walk either way, which is why the 155-file ticket is FASTER than
the 25-file one (fewer/shallower trees to walk in its history slice). That is the shape
change: the cost stopped being per-signed-event.

The mechanism is confirmed as diagnosed — it is the pathspec, not the process count. A
per-file GLOB forces git to evaluate the match at every commit; a bare directory prefix
lets git prune whole trees. The cost is now per-COMPACTION rather than per-signed-event,
so it stops scaling with the number of signed events.

## How equivalence was proved

Attribution feeds `verify-authorship`, so equivalence was asserted, not assumed:

1. **Against real history** — the measurement above compares the batched map to
   `resolve_event_commit` for EVERY event of each ticket on the real 71k-commit store: 0
   mismatches.
2. **Against the off-first-parent case explicitly** — a fixture whose history contains an
   event added on BOTH sides of a merge (the shape a store gets when two clones write the
   same event and sync). The merge is TREESAME to both parents for that path, so default
   simplification follows only the first parent and answers with the MAINLINE add, while
   `--full-history` sees the older side-branch add. The test asserts both resolvers return
   the side-branch commit AND that the simplified query returns something DIFFERENT — so
   the fixture provably exercises the case `--full-history` exists for, and cannot silently
   stop doing so.
3. **At the call site** — the ledger `_build_authorship_ledger` produces is compared
   entry-by-entry to the old per-event loop (`resolve_event_commit` then the global
   `resolve_position_commit` fallback).
4. **Fail-closed** — a forced empty map (any git failure) is asserted to fall back to the
   per-event resolver with unchanged shas, so batching can only ever cost time, never a
   wrong or missing commit.

`--full-history` is kept, the event TYPE stays a non-input (keyed by position), lock
semantics/acquisition/scope are untouched, and the ledger stays INSIDE the lock — so R2's
race never has to be risked.

## R3 — the skip, and why no floor

Approved after the operator's design answer that the load is INTERMITTENT. Detection uses
the existing mechanism: `write_lock_is_busy()` is the same two legs `acquire` takes, in
the same order, with a zero deadline. Both legs are probed (an fcntl-only probe would read
a store held by a bash-era or flock-less writer as free), the fcntl leg is released in a
`finally` whether or not the mkdir leg is taken, a successful mkdir probe removes the dir
immediately, and the probe fails OPEN so a probe failure degrades to today's behaviour
rather than suppressing work on a free store.

Skipping is a no-op for correctness, asserted end-to-end against a real store with a real
second holder: the close still succeeds, the event log is byte-for-byte unchanged, and the
next uncontended compaction folds exactly what the skipped one would have (same reduced
state). No forced-after-N-skips floor, per the intermittent-load answer; the skip is logged
at WARNING with the holder so a compaction that never runs again cannot be silent.

## What is NOT closed by this

* R3's floor question stands if the load ever becomes sustained.
* The acquire-budget shape is untouched: a `LockTimeout` is still terminal and lossy
  (option 1 of the earlier assessment — durable spool on timeout — remains unimplemented).
  The measured claim is that R1 removes the incident class, not that loss is now
  impossible.
* Post-R1 re-measurement under the 6-writer harness has NOT been rerun; that is the next
  evidence needed before judging whether per-ticket locking is required.

compiled_state.description:
# compact-on-close holds the store write lock for MINUTES, starving concurrent writers — and "isolated" worktrees share one store

## The two facts together are the defect

### 1. The worktrees are NOT isolated — they symlink to ONE store

`/Users/joeoakhart/agent-5200-diag/.tickets-tracker` is a **symlink** to
`/Users/joeoakhart/rebar/.tickets-tracker`. So is `/Users/joeoakhart/probe-status-e34a/.tickets-tracker`.
All three resolve to the same path and to the **same lock inode (420945058)**.
`lock.canonical_tracker` (`_store/lock.py:124-127`) realpaths deliberately so that they contend on one
lock — which is correct behaviour for correctness, and means every parallel agent session serialises
through a single write lock even though each believes it has its own worktree.

Two live `rebar transition ... closed` processes were running against this store during the incident
(from `agent-5200-diag` and `probe-status-e34a`).

### 2. compact-on-close holds that lock across an entire reduce + retire + git commit

`_commands/compact.py:178` takes the same write lock and holds it across the whole critical section
(`compact.py:186` onward), and it is invoked right after every close at
`_commands/transition_close.py:92-104`.

Measured from the tracker's own git log: a **2m17s gap** with nothing landing between
`2a8f02ce14 SIGNATURE e39f` (12:28:38) and `b2e28d2273 COMPACT e39f` (12:30:55). The next commit is
d582's STATUS at 12:30:56 — one second after the compaction released.

### The consequence

A concurrent writer's 60s lock budget (`lock.py:73-74`: 30s x 2 attempts) is consumed entirely inside
one compaction window. That is what dropped a durable record in
[rebar:ab54-f19f-d5bd-422c] — the close's PASS `COMPLETION_VERDICT` sidecar got its single 60s shot
during the gap and lost it.

`flock` is also not FIFO, so a waiter can additionally be starved by a stream of short writers rather
than by one long holder.

Corroborating symptom: `2bc7-d77b-641c-42aa` carries **two** PASS sidecars (12:34:22 and 12:36:31) —
a close that had to be retried under the same contention.

### Diagnosability gap found along the way

**The lock records no holder identity that survives contention.** The fcntl leg (`lock.py:552`) records
no pid at all, and the only owner stamp lives in `.ticket-write.lock.d/owner` (`lock.py:36`), which is
removed on release — so a timed-out waiter cannot say who blocked it. The holder above was identified by
inferring from the commit timeline, not from any recorded pid. A `LockTimeout` that cannot name the
holder is expensive to diagnose under fleet load.

Also observed, separately: `llm/enrich_drain.py:243-251`'s "cheap gate" logs
`enrich drain gate check took 300-800ms (> 20 ms budget)` on nearly every command against this
3174-ticket store, and `overlap_drain=async` detaches drain CHILD processes that write events
(`enrich_drain.py:254-256`), making them additional lock contenders. None committed inside the measured
gap, so they are not the holder here.

### Residue

An untracked `.tickets-tracker/.tmp-event-lpusw0uh` (mtime 10:42) predates this incident and belongs to
some other failed or killed write. `event_append.py:470-472` does unlink the staging temp on
`LockTimeout`, so this is from a different failure mode — worth sweeping and worth knowing that
something leaves temps behind.

## Acceptance Criteria

- [ ] compaction no longer holds the store write lock across its whole reduce + git-commit section —
      either it takes the lock only for the final swap, or it yields between phases, measured by the
      commit-gap shrinking under a concurrent-writer test
- [ ] a `LockTimeout` names the holder: the lock records an owner (pid + worktree) that a timed-out
      waiter can read and report, so diagnosis does not require timeline inference
- [ ] concurrent close from two worktrees sharing one store does not drop a durable record — asserted
      by a test that closes from two processes against one tracker
- [ ] the shared-store-by-symlink topology is documented where agents are told to use a fresh worktree,
      since "isolated worktree" currently implies an isolated store and does not get one
- [ ] the stray `.tmp-event-*` residue is swept, and its source failure mode is identified or explicitly
      recorded as unknown

## Testing

    pytest tests/unit -k "lock or compact or concurren" -q
    make lint && make typecheck

A concurrent-writer reproduction is the load-bearing test: two processes closing tickets against one
canonical tracker, asserting both closes land every durable record. Without it this is a timing bug that
only reappears under fleet load.
